title: Soft-fidelity ladders: mini-model failover + token-priority eviction for graceful OOM recovery
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Under broad traffic bursts with diverse request shapes we observe GPU OOMs that cause hard failures or long tail retries. Current mitigation (large-model fallback or full KV eviction) is too coarse: it either loses fidelity completely or causes expensive cold-starts for heavier models. We need a reactive yet low-friction recovery strategy that preserves useful output while avoiding hard OOMs.

Goal: Implement a multi-pronged graceful-degradation mechanism: (1) a soft "fidelity ladder" where requests can be degraded along quality tiers (reduced max tokens, reduced sampling compute, and distilled mini-models) without full cancellation; (2) token-priority aware KV eviction that trims cold or low-impact KV entries first; (3) a coordinated retry orchestration that attempts rapid lightweight retries against lower-fidelity tiers and only escalates to heavier fallbacks when necessary. The overall aim is to reduce hard OOM rate by >= 70% on stress workloads while keeping mean output quality loss <= 15% (measured by existing eval prompts).

Design summary:
- Fidelity tiers: native (full model, full settings) -> trimmed (max tokens -25%, lower temperature / smaller top-k) -> micro-model (distilled 1.5–3B variant) -> compressed-stream (stream token baseline, aggressive prefix caching reclaim). The platform will expose a per-request "degrade_budget" integer that indicates how many degradation steps are permitted.
- Token-priority KV eviction: extend KV metadata with an access-frequency and recency score (decayed per-second). Eviction will remove entries below a dynamic threshold computed from current free GPU bytes and upstream degrade_budget. Cold tokens (low score) get evicted first; pinned hot prefixes are protected. This is incremental eviction (small batches) to avoid spiky reclaim costs.
- Retry orchestration: when admission or OOM risk is detected during batch admission or during runtime, the request can be fast-retried in-place with next fidelity tier. Retry uses exponential jitter backoff tuned for our batch admission window (base 10ms, max 250ms in practice). Retries are bounded by a per-request retry budget.
- Memory budgeting and slot reservation: each worker maintains a lightweight per-slot reserved headroom measured in bytes; batch admission checks aggregated headroom before accepting large max-token requests. If headroom not available, admission attempts degrade the highest-cost request(s) first rather than rejecting the entire batch.

Implementation tasks (high level):
- Runtime: extend admission controller to support degrade_budget and per-request cost model; integrate soft-degrade decision path.
- KV cache: add lightweight score metadata and incremental eviction loop with async reclaim. Provide observability metrics for eviction rate and miss patterns.
- Models: onboard and validate distilled micro-model variants for critical families (gpt-family and llama-family). Provide a mapping table for which micro-model to use as fallback per tenant.
- Orchestration: implement retry coordinator with jitter/backoff, and tie into existing tracing for causal continuity (so clients can correlate retries).
- Console/Telemetry: add dials to view how often each degrade tier is used, per-tenant fidelity loss, and OOM avoidance counts.

Acceptance criteria:
- Hard OOMs on synthetic stress tests reduced by >= 70% compared to baseline.
- Average request latency increase for degraded requests < 30% vs native for the same effective output.
- Mean eval quality loss across our platform regression suite < 15% when accounting for degraded outputs across test prompt sets.
- Feature flags and rollout paths exist for Canary -> Platform -> Global rollout.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Quality regressions for latency-sensitive or safety-critical flows: mitigate via per-tenant opt-out and ability to pin model/version.
- Extra complexity in admission logic increases maintenance cost and risk of subtle bugs; mitigate with defensive unit/integration tests and a staged rollout.
- Micro-model cold starts and compatibility mismatches: validate tokenizer/IO parity during onboarding and add auto-fallback to alternative micro-model if mismatch detected.

References and artifacts:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/soft-fidelity-ladders
- Micro-model benchmark spreadsheet (Drive): https://drive.google.com/drive/fake/micro-model-benchmarks
- Initial perf dashboard (internal): https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/oom/fidelity-ladder-canary

Rollout plan:
1) Unit and integration tests + localbench harness (2 weeks)
2) Canary on a small Dedicated pool with synthetic burst tests and live traffic siphon (1 week)
3) Evaluate telemetry, tune eviction thresholds and degrade budgets (1 week)
4) Gradual ramp to all pools with tenant opt-in for non-default aggressive degrade.

Estimated effort: 5 engineer-weeks (split runtime, models, infra).

2026-03-11 — Miguel Alvarez: Spike complete for per-request cost model; dataset shows 40% of memory pressure comes from a small fraction (~8%) of very long max-token requests. Proposed degrade_budget of 2 as sensible default.
